Question: Why is atmosphere not stratified when it is composed of gases of different weights eg CO2 is heavier than O. CO2 should form a layer below that of O. Rather, there is a mixture of these gases that we breathe in?
Answer: Gas molecules are in constant movement - at quite high speeds. The average speed varies with temperature and the mass of the gas molecule. The average speed increases with temperature and decreases with increasing molecular mass. The speed of individual molecules also varies - some are moving faster than the average speed and some slower. The average speed can be calculated from the equation: v= Square root(3 x R x T/M) where v = average speed in meters per second R = gas constant - which is 8.31447 J mol¯1 K¯1 T = the temperature in degrees Kelvin M = molecular mass in Kilograms per mole Let us calculate the speed of nitrogen molecules at a temperature of 293 degrees K (approximately 20 degrees Celsius or 68 degrees F) The molar mass of nitrogen (N2) is 0.028 Kg/mol Therefore in this case: v= Square root ( 3 x 8.31447 x 293/0.028) v = 511 meters/sec = 1,142 miles per hour The oxygen molecules are a bit heavier at 0.032 Kg/mol v= Square root( 3 x 8.31447 x 293/0.032) = 478 m/s or 1,069 mph Carbon dioxide molecules are heavier still at 0.044 Kg/mol v= Square root( 3 x 8.31447 x 293/0.044) = 408 m/sec or 912 mph The high speed at which the individual molecules are moving accounts for why the three gasses are well mixed in the lower atmosphere. The carbon dioxide levels do fall with increasing altitude, but quite slowly. Here are some actual measurements. At much higher altitudes, the gas concentrations change more dramatically. Molecules heading upwards are slowed by gravity and fall back towards Earth. A further reason why the atmosphere becomes more stratified with altitude is that the molecules become less crowded. At sea level they are constantly jostling each other, and the mean free path is a few nanometers. High in the atmosphere the mean free path can be kilometers long.

Question: Where do Earth's major river systems end up?
Answer: Most river systems end up in the world’s oceans. Click the map below to enlarge. There are some exceptions. The Nile system ends up in the Mediterranean - which connects to the Atlantic Ocean. The Mississippi and the Rio Grande end up in the Gulf of Mexico, which also connects to the Atlantic Ocean. Question: What is the scientific explanation for how life started on Earth? If there is no scientific explanation, what are some theories?
Answer: Life on Earth started a long time ago, so there is not much evidence left of exactly how it started. This is in sharp contrast to the evidence for biological evolution, which is still continuing and going on all around us. However, we can gain some clues from the evidence that we have. A clue that does come to us from the early days of the Earth is that life started relatively early. The earliest fossils date from 3.7 billion years ago - just 800 million years after the formation of the Earth. And during most of those 800 million years the environment would have been extremely hostile, with high temperatures, volcanic eruptions and bombardment by asteroids. By contrast it took another 3 billion years for multi-cellular life to appear. This suggests that single cell life can appear relatively easily. Another clue that came to light in 1952 was the famous Miller-Urey experiment that showed that amino acids - the building blocks for proteins - could be formed by lightening acting on the early Earth atmosphere. This suggests the “biotic soup” theory first articulated by Charles Darwin himself in a letter to James Hooker. "But if (and oh what a big if) we could conceive in some warm little pond with all sorts of ammonia and phosphoric salts, light, heat, electricity etcetera present, that a protein compound was chemically formed, ready to undergo still more complex changes [..] " However the search for exactly how complex life arose on Earth involves much more than biochemistry. The chart above comes from a paper at One of the most interesting theories on the origin of life is explained in a wonderful book Seven Clues to the Origin of Life by Alexander Graham Cairns-Smith. Cairns-Smith treats the investigation as a detective story and frequently refers to the Sherlock Holmes dictum that it is the puzzling and paradoxical features of a case that hold the most clues to solving it. For example, there is the question why so many biological molecules are chiral - they are different from their mirror image and left-handed molecules predominate in life. Cairns -Smith’s conclusion is that life originated in clay minerals. You should get his book to read the details.

Question: Does the Cambrian explosion provide evidence for intelligent design?
Answer: “Evidence” is too strong a word - but the amazing diversification of life at the beginning of the Cambrian is at least suggestive of the possibility of intelligent design. The concept is hotly denied by nearly all biologists, but their arguments have a few holes in them. A large number (perhaps 85%) of the phyla recognised by biologists came into existence at the beginning of the Cambrian period. For most of the Earth’s history, encompassing billions of years, the only evidence of life is of microbial life, most famously the stromatolite microbial mats dating back 4 billion years. Then, just before the Cambrian, there are two sets of fossilised evidence of multicellular organisms. These are the Ediacaran fauna and the small shelly fauna. The Ediacaran fauna have been found at several sites around the world, in the form of impressions in fine grained rock. They had no bony structures, and they appear to have gone extinct and left no descendants. The small shelly fauna left small shells, which may have been part of larger creatures. Then immediately after this, in the early Cambrian, we have a sudden proliferations of all kinds of new fossils. It certainly appears in the fossil record like an “explosion”. Even Charles Darwin was aware of this issue. He said “To the question of why we do not find rich fossiliferous deposits belonging to these…periods prior to the Cambrian system, I can give no satisfactory answer”. To explain this Cambrian explosion it is said that wasn’t really an explosion, but more of a slow fuse as it lasted 20 million years. However most of the new phyla came into existence in the early Cambrian - perhaps over 5 million years or less. It is said that molecular evidence from modern phyla suggests that they diverged well before the Cambrian explosion. However if this is the case, why didn’t they leave fossil remains? It is said that they didn’t leave fossils because they hadn’t developed hard body parts. But the Ediacaran fauna didn’t have hard body parts either, and they left fossils. It is said that chemical conditions weren’t right to preserve calcareous parts - but the small shellies left preserved parts. I think that it’s possible that there was intervention which speeded up evolution. This was no supernatural intervention by a divine omniscient being. Rather it was the work of tinkerers. The failed experiments of the Ediacaran and small shelly faunas show that that could have been their initial work. Intervention would have made changes to genes in different phyla, which molecular scientists now interpret as earlier diversification. The incorporation of prokaryotes into the eukaryote cells as organelles like the mitochondria also suggests tinkering. In case you think this theory is far fetched, it has been suggested by sober scientists that humans might one day do the same thing. An article in the usually staid journal Astrophysics and Space Science (Developing ecospheres on transiently habitable planets: the genesis project) suggests that humans may one day attempt to speed up evolution on promising exoplanets. If serious scientists suggest such a course of action, why couldn’t it have happened on Earth? It seems to me that opposition to the idea any kind of intelligent input to species diversification in the Cambrian explosion is more ideological based than evidence based.

Question: What are the percentages of hydrogen and helium in Earth’s atmosphere?
Answer: By number of atoms, hydrogen makes up 0.269% of the Earth’s atmosphere. Because hydrogen is the lightest element, by mass its contribution is much less - 0.0093%. This still amounts to quite a lot of hydrogen - 1.4 trillion tons. Most of this hydrogen is in the form of water vapor. A lesser amount is in the form of methane. Elemental hydrogen makes up just 0.0000550% of the atoms in the atmosphere and just 0.0000038% of the mass of the atmosphere. Helium makes up 0.000522% by number of atoms and 0.000072% by mass. All the helium is in its monatomic elemental form

Question: Why did I just read from Washington post that Earth’s inner core seems to be slowing its spin?
Answer: Knowledge of the nature of the inner parts of the Earth is gleaned from various sources, some rather speculative. The density of the Earth shows that it can’t be all rock - there must be something denser. The most common denser element found in meteorites is iron, so the assumption is that the dense core of the Earth consists of iron, along with associated other elements. Another clue is given by the study of seismic waves. These waves are generated by earthquakes, nuclear tests and even mine blasting. There are numerous seismic stations around the world. Valuable information is generate by the precise timing at which waves from a particular event arrive at different stations. There are several different kinds of waves. The most important are P (pressure) waves and S (shear) waves. In P waves particles vibrate in the direction of travel . Sound is a P wave. S waves vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel. Light is an S wave. (Ocean waves are surface waves - a third form. Much earthquake damage results from surface waves but they are less important for seismology). The important difference between S and P waves is that P waves can transmit through liquids, but S waves are limited to solids. This is how seismologists first found that the core of the Earth is liquid. In 1936 the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann used more sophisticated analysis to show that the inner core of the Earth is solid. Seismologists usually call layers where there are abrupt changes in seismic behaviour ‘discontinuities’. By rights the boundary between the inner solid and outer liquid core should have been named after Inge as the Lehmann discontinuity. However there was already another discontinuity named after her, so it’s usually called the Bullen discontinuity. Reproducing the conditions at the centre of the Earth in the laboratory is very hard. There is some support for the idea that the solid core is crystalline pure iron. Latent heat released by the solidification of iron under high pressure would make the Bullen discontinuity very hot. In 1996 further more sophisticated analysis of how arrival times of seismic waves had changed over the years caused Geophysicist Paul Richards of Columbia University to propose that the solid core is rotating slightly faster than the outer parts of the planet. The difference in speed is tiny - about 1 degree per year. (Note the Earth rotates 365 x 360 = 131,400 degrees in a year.) Now geophysicists Xiaodong Song of Peking University in Beijing and Paul Richards of the Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory in New York have published a paper that proposes that the inner core rotation has slowed slightly and is falling behind that of the rest of the planet. They propose an oscillation over a 70 year time period. Once again the difference in rotation speeds is tiny. Question: Why is aluminum more expensive than magnesium, even though it’s a “rare earth” element while magnesium isn't?
Answer: Neither magnesium nor aluminum is a “rare earth” (lanthanide) element. Element 12, Magnesium is in Group 2 of the Periodic Table as an alkaline earth metal and element 13, aluminum, is in group 13 as a post transition metal. Both take about 15 kilowatt hours of electricity to make one kilogram of metal.
